A National Natural Landmarks (NNL) is a natural area that contains an outstanding example of the nation's natural history—either biological, geological, or both. It is officially designated by the Secretary of the Interior. What does "national significance" mean? Experts evaluate sites based on how well they represent a natural feature (illustrative value) and how well the site is preserved (condition of the resource. The U.S. National Science Foundation's Research Traineeship Program is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary or convergence research areas, through a comprehensive traineeship model that is innovative, evidence-based and aligned with changing workforce and research needs. What do trainees research? Traineeships can focus on any high priority research, but specific areas can range in topics from artificial intelligence and quantum information science and engineering to the six research areas within NSF's 10 Big Ideas that serve the nation's future. What is convergence research? Convergence research is driven by a specific and compelling problem where there is deep and intentional integration across disciplines. The goal of convergence research is to discover and develop new frameworks, paradigms, or disciplines that address critical questions or challenges. Who can create an NSF Research Traineeship? Accredited institutions of higher education, including community colleges, may apply to launch an NSF Research Traineeship at their institution. The FAO Global Action on One Country One Priority Product (OCOP) has four main objectives: facilitate the development of sustainable and inclusive value chains of agricultural products, in particular for family farming and smallholder farmers; support Members through the implementation of the Country Programming Frameworks (CPF); strengthen the implementation of the FAO Strategic Framework 2022-2031, especially the Four Betters (Better Production, Better Nutrition, a Better Environment, and a Better Life); and contribute to achieving the UN 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), in particular SDG 1 (No poverty), SDG 2 (Zero hunger) and SDG 10 (Reduced inequality). The ultimate goal of the OCOP is to support the transition to MORE efficient, inclusive, resilient and sustainable agrifood systems. pages.text: Freya Bell: Wales centre a major doubt for 2027 Women's Six Nations - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Freya Bell was carried off the field during the second half of Wales' 17-0 victory in Tokyo Published 17 November 2026 Wales centre Freya Bell has been ruled out of the upcoming Celtic Challenge and is a major doubt for the 2027 Women's Six Nations after having knee surgery. The 22-year-old suffered a serious injury in Wales' first WXV Global Series victory over Japan last month. It is a blow to Wales, with Bell impressing since making her debut against England in last year's Six Nations and starting the first three WXV games ahead of last season's Wales player of the year Courtney Keight. Writing on social media, the Cardiff Met and former Harlequins player said: "Not the season I had hoped for, but very grateful for the opportunities I have had so far. "Time to get rehabbing for now. Diolch for all the love and support." The Celtic Challenge runs from 5 December to 27 March, with Wales opening their Six Nations on 10 April. pages.title: From 22,000 Miles Up, This Satellite Tracks Airborne Health Threats Almost in Real Time
pages.description: The new instrument, called TEMPO, captures hourly snapshots of the pollutants swirling in the daytime atmosphere over North America—“chemical weather” reports that are helpful to public health researchers and government officials
pages.text: From 22,000 Miles Up, This Satellite Tracks Airborne Health Threats Almost in Real Time Skip to main content Smoke from massive wildfires in Canada engulfed the New York City skyline, reducing visibility and casting an orange haze over city on July 16, 2026. Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images In early August, the skies above Portland, Oregon, took on an increasingly familiar sepia tint as easterly winds wafted plumes of gas and smoke from wildfires into the air over the city. At one point Portland’s air quality was ranked worst in the world , leading to the closure of summer camps and public pools and the cancellation of outdoor concerts. In a summer of intense heat and wildfires, similar scenarios played out in cities across North America—New York, Denver, Chicago, Toledo. Above it all, a satellite recorded the dynamic swirl of gases and particulates fueling these air quality crises. From a vantage point 22,000 miles above the equator, the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) satellite, a joint effort by NASA and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, has provided near-real-time hourly snapshots of pollutants originating, migrating and dissipating in the daytime atmosphere over North America since September 2025. Whereas previous pollution-monitoring satellites offered only one or two daily snapshots of air quality, this ongoing, continent-scale picture has helped researchers and regulators better understand and respond to some of the most unpredictable and uncontrollable pollutants in the atmosphere. Thilanka Perera; Getty Images By Lorna Parkes Published October 9, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Taking cocktails by the beach has never been so exciting. I’m trying to admire the bruised sunset, the frothing of the waves near my feet, the lychee-topped creation in my hand — but there’s a noise coming from the undergrowth that tells me my attention should be elsewhere. The word ‘elephant’ ripples across the beach, bouncing from table to table, as a massive rump comes into view. It’s close enough to ogle, but far enough away for us to not need an emergency evacuation. The hotel manager stands on top of a sand dune, shifting uneasily from one foot to the other, as the creature ambles on its way, totally absorbed in finding its own dinner as we wait for ours. In Sri Lanka’s south east, unexpected visitors don’t wait for a convenient moment to make their entrance. Especially when you’re staying at a hotel in Yala National Park’s buffer zone — the transitional area between the country’s most popular park and urban development on the southern coast. The second chairman of the Authority was Robert H. Hinckley, shown above with Vannevar Bush and Orville Wright. Hinckley was the force behind the Civilian Pilot Training Program (CPTP). Beginning on a regular basis in the 1939-40 school year, the CPTP graduated thousands of new pilots as a means of strengthening the nation for possible war. After the Pearl Harbor attack, the program was renamed the War Training Service (WTS). (CAA photos from Patricia Strickland's The "Putt-Putt" Air Force, a 1974 FAA publication.) pages.text: From Farm to Future | National Geographic Paid Content for Cargill ENVIRONMENT From Farm to Future Two farming families, thousands of miles apart, show how long-term resilience and strong relationships help them plan for what comes next. 14:24 Behind every meal are farmers, families, and a network of connections helping to keep food on our tables. Video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated November 13, 2026 Every meal begins long before we sit down to eat. Somewhere, a farmer is deciding what to grow, what to raise, and how to prepare for a future they can never fully predict. Months—sometimes years—before food reaches our plates, choices are being made that will help shape the meals we eat tomorrow. Those choices aren’t simple. Farmers invest before they know what prices they'll receive. They make plans before they know what the weather will bring. And they care for land they hope will support not only the next harvest, but the next generation. For most of us, this interconnected network of decisions remains largely out of sight. We walk into a grocery store and expect to find the shelves stocked, rarely pausing to think about the people, land, and relationships that make it all possible. Across the world, more than 600 million farmers are producing food for a global population of over eight billion. Their operations may look different, but they share a common responsibility: growing, raising, and producing the food people rely on every day. The contract between them is represented using KTIR (Kernel Tile IR), an MLIR representation built on a data-parallel view of the accelerator, in which every compute tile can see every memory and a single logical tensor can live spread across several cores’ scratchpads. A new open-source Dataflow Scheduler consumes KTIR and turns each tile’s work into a dataflow pipeline: it splits the kernel into programs, starts from a simple load → compute → store pipeline, routes every transfer through the memory hierarchy given in an architecture description, and expands that pipeline into a nested, double-buffered, multi-instance schedule. The output of the scheduler is represented using DataflowIR , an MLIR intermediate representation that Spyre’s device-specific stages use to produce SpyreCode , a symbolic SpyreBinary plus a job plan that the Spyre runtime prepares once and launches many times, filling in tensor addresses and shapes at launch. By Virginia Hughes Published March 13, 2013 • 9 min read The first draft of the Neanderthal genome, published in 2010, came with some titillating news. It showed that 50,000 years ago, these ancient hominids interbred with the ancestors of many modern humans. If you have European or Asian ancestry, an estimated 1 to 4 percent of your DNA came from Neanderthals. On the off chance that your mind hasn’t gone there, allow me: Our ancestors, looking pretty much like we do today, had sex with the short, extremely muscular, big-nosed, big-browed, big-headed Neanderthals. Were the differences between the two species mostly physical, with shared intellectual and cultural pursuits the subjects of their pillow talk? Or were Neanderthals violent, mute, and stupid, as so often depicted in popular culture ? Or something in between? Neanderthals almost certainly weren’t as brutish as assumed a century ago. Anthropologists now know that they used tools, made art, and may have talked . Still, nobody fully knows how their brains worked, or how their thinking was different from ours. The uncertainty is understandable considering the evidence. All scientists have to go on are the fossilized skulls the Neanderthals left behind. pages.description: Scientists show direct link between winter ice cover in Barents and Kara seas and summer drought in eastern Europe and central Asia
pages.text: From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas Frontiers | Science news Science news Climate action From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas What causes summer droughts, like the severe dry conditions seen across much of Europe in 2026? Here, climate scientists have shown in records stretching over more than a century that summer droughts in Eastern Europe and Central Asia tended to follow upon winters with less-than-average sea ice in the Barents Sea and Kara Sea, two rapidly warming regions in the Arctic. This pattern remained after accounting for the long-term rise in atmospheric CO2, while additional analyses supported a one-way causal link. The authors propose a plausible mechanism by which less winter ice favors stagnant weather and warm, dry air along a ‘drought corridor’ from eastern Romania to western Kazakhstan. Unusually little winter sea ice may thus offer an early clue that the risk of summer drought is higher there. This summer, with its scarce rainfall and repeated heatwaves, witnessed one of the most severe droughts in European history since 1540. Abbreviations should be avoided within the title. Witty and creative titles are welcome, but only if relevant and within measure. Authors should avoid: titles that are a mere question without giving the answer unambitious titles, for example starting with 'Towards,' 'A description of,' 'A characterization of' or 'Preliminary study on' vague titles, for example starting with 'Role of', 'Link between', or 'Effect of' that do not specify the role, link, or effect including terms that are out of place, for example the taxonomic affiliation apart from species name. pages.text: Frontiers in Big Data | About Skip to main content Editor guidelines Frontiers' collaborative peer review is unique and quality-focused. Read on for a guide for reviewers on what to expect of our peer review process. What is Frontiers' peer review model? Frontiers operates a single-anonymized model during the review process. This means the reviewers know who the authors are in order to offer a full assessment within the context of their research and to ensure they can avoid any potential competing interests in accepting a review invitation. Frontiers also believes that reviewers should be acknowledged for their work in conducting peer review. We believe in transparency and ensuring no bias during the peer review process. This is why we disclose the name of all endorsing reviewers upon publication, for every article we publish. What to expect from our collaborative peer review Our peer review platform is collaborative: it unites authors, reviewers, and the handling editor in a direct online dialog, enabling quick iterations and facilitating consensus. Editors and reviewers work with the authors to improve their manuscript. Independent review phase Once a reviewer accepts the invitation to review, they are sent an email with a link to the online review forum. In the review forum, they can access and review the manuscript and supporting documents. During this first review phase the reviewers assess the paper independently from each other and the authors. pages.text: Frontiers | History Skip to main content History Where it all started Frontiers was founded in 2007 by Henry Markram and Kamila Markram , neuroscientists from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (EPFL) in Lausanne, Switzerland. Henry and Kamila launched Frontiers with a vision to make science open, peer review rigorous, transparent, and efficient and harness the power of technology to truly serve researchers’ needs. Initially starting in the field of neuroscience, Frontiers now spans hundreds of academic disciplines and is one of the most cited and largest research publishers in the world. Dr Kamila Markram speaks about open science and the vision behind Frontiers at TEDx Brussels in 2017. The people behind Frontiers 2007. Frontiers is launched as a not-for-profit foundation, then relying on philanthropic donations to operate. The foundation continues to exist today, supporting purely philanthropic initiatives, including Frontiers for Young Minds and the Frontiers Planet Prize . 2008. Operations are taken over by Frontiers Media SA, a company created by the founders to enable long-term economic and operational sustainability. The gold open access business model is adopted. The same year, Frontiers receives an investment from Kaltroco, the private holding company of the Koltes family. They strongly support the vision to make science open and their investment kick-starts the ensuing growth of Frontiers. 2013. pages.text: Frontiers | Mission Skip to main content About Frontiers Frontiers is one of the world’s largest and most impactful research publishers, dedicated to making peer-reviewed, quality-certified science openly accessible. With over three million researchers across 222 community-led journals covering approximately 1,700 academic disciplines, we provide researchers with a trusted, cutting-edge, AI-powered open science platform to rigorously review their findings and maximize the dissemination of their discoveries.​ As an open access pioneer, we actively drive the global transition to open science, working with researchers, universities, educators, policymakers, and businesses. Watch: Science Unlocked, a documentary hosted by CNBC, spotlights Frontiers' mission to make science open and the powerful role this approach plays in accelerating breakthroughs across health, climate resilience, technology, the economy, and society. Our mission Our mission is to make science open – so that scientists can collaborate better and innovate faster to deliver the solutions that enable healthy lives on a healthy planet. Research is the foundation of modern society and it’s thanks to advances in science that we enjoy longer, healthier and more prosperous lives than ever before in human history. We want to make science even more powerful by ensuring it is openly available. This way, society will be able to generate more knowledge and accelerate innovation, health and prosperity for all. However, the increasing computational complexity, memory requirements, and energy consumption of these models pose significant challenges to their practical deployment, especially in resource-constrained and real-world environments. Developing compact, efficient, and adaptive AI models has therefore become a critical research direction for bridging the gap between advanced AI algorithms and practical applications. This Research Topic, entitled "Model Compression and Efficient Learning for Real-World Systems," aims to bring together cutting-edge research on model compression, computationally efficient learning, and resource-aware AI systems.
